questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a biofuel from a fossil fuel?
options: A biofuel releases no carbon dioxide when burned; a fossil fuel releases a great deal
A biofuel is always a gas; a fossil fuel is always a liquid or a solid at room temperature
A biofuel is made from recently living matter; a fossil fuel formed over millions of years
A biofuel contains no carbon; a fossil fuel is made mostly of carbon and hydrogen
questions.explanation: Biofuels such as bioethanol, biodiesel and biogas come from recent biomass, so they are renewable on a human timescale. Fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms over millions of years. Both contain carbon and release carbon dioxide when burned.

questions.stem: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
options: Biogas
Biodiesel
Natural gas
Bioethanol
questions.explanation: Natural gas, mostly methane, formed from ancient buried organic matter. Biogas is also mostly methane, but it is produced now by anaerobic digestion of waste, so it is a biofuel.

questions.stem: How is bioethanol usually produced?
options: By reacting vegetable oils with methanol and a catalyst
By anaerobic digestion of animal manure in a sealed tank
By fermenting sugars from crops such as sugar cane with yeast
By fractional distillation of crude oil at an oil refinery
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Reacting vegetable oil with methanol makes biodiesel, and anaerobic digestion makes biogas.

questions.stem: How is biodiesel made?
options: By heating coal without air so that it gives off gaseous hydrocarbons
By reacting vegetable oils or animal fats with methanol to form esters
By fermenting glucose with yeast and then distilling off the product
By cracking the heavy fractions of crude oil into smaller molecules
questions.explanation: Triglycerides in oils and fats react with methanol (transesterification) to give methyl esters, which are biodiesel, and glycerol. Fermentation makes ethanol, and cracking is a refinery process for fossil fuels.

questions.stem: The heat of combustion of methane (CH₄, M = 16.0 g/mol) is 890 kJ/mol. How much energy is released per gram?
options: 890 kJ/g
questions.explanation: Energy per gram = 890 / 16.0 = 55.6 kJ/g. Multiplying by the molar mass instead gives 14 240, and dividing the molar mass by the heat of combustion gives 0.018.

questions.stem: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH, M = 46.0 g/mol) has a heat of combustion of 1360 kJ/mol. How much energy is released by burning 100 g of ethanol completely?
options: 2.96 x 10³ kJ
1.36 x 10⁵ kJ
1.36 x 10³ kJ
questions.explanation: n = 100 / 46.0 = 2.17 mol, so energy = 2.17 x 1360 = 2.96 x 10³ kJ. Multiplying 1360 by 100 treats grams as moles, and 3.38 kJ comes from dividing 100 x 46.0 by 1360.

questions.stem: Per gram, octane (C₈H₁₈) releases 47.9 kJ and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) releases 29.6 kJ. Which explanation for the difference is best?
options: Octane is a fossil fuel, and fossil fuels always contain stored solar energy
Octane burns incompletely, which releases more energy than complete combustion
Ethanol is partly oxidised already: its oxygen adds mass but no energy
Ethanol molecules are smaller, so they contain fewer bonds per gram to break
questions.explanation: An ethanol molecule already contains an oxygen atom bonded to carbon, so part of its mass is oxygen that contributes no energy on combustion. Incomplete combustion releases less energy, not more.

questions.stem: How many grams of methane (M = 16.0 g/mol, heat of combustion 890 kJ/mol) must be burned completely to release 5000 kJ?
questions.explanation: n = 5000 / 890 = 5.62 mol, and mass = 5.62 x 16.0 = 89.9 g. Stopping at 5.62 gives moles rather than grams.

questions.stem: Heats of combustion: methane CH₄ 890 kJ/mol, ethanol C₂H₅OH 1360 kJ/mol, octane C₈H₁₈ 5460 kJ/mol. Which fuel releases the most energy per mole of CO₂ produced?
options: Methane
Ethanol
Octane
All release the same
questions.explanation: Per mole of CO₂: methane 890 / 1 = 890 kJ, ethanol 1360 / 2 = 680 kJ, octane 5460 / 8 = 683 kJ. Octane releases the most per mole of fuel, but methane releases the most per unit of CO₂.

questions.stem: Ethanol releases 29.6 kJ/g and has a density of 0.789 g/mL; octane releases 47.9 kJ/g and has a density of 0.703 g/mL. About how much energy does each release per litre?
options: Ethanol 23.4 MJ/L; octane 33.7 MJ/L
Ethanol 37.5 MJ/L; octane 68.1 MJ/L
Ethanol 29.6 MJ/L; octane 47.9 MJ/L
Ethanol 33.7 MJ/L; octane 23.4 MJ/L
questions.explanation: One litre of ethanol has mass 789 g, so 789 x 29.6 = 23 400 kJ = 23.4 MJ; octane gives 703 x 47.9 = 33 700 kJ = 33.7 MJ. Dividing by the density instead of multiplying gives the larger values.

questions.stem: Students heat 250 g of water by 20.0 degrees C using an ethanol burner and find 0.80 g of ethanol was used. Using q = mcΔT with c = 4.18 J/g/°C, what energy per gram do they calculate, and why is it below the data value of 29.6 kJ/g?
options: 26.1 kJ/g; some heat is lost to the surroundings, not the water
26.1 kJ/g; the ethanol releases more heat than expected in the open air
20.9 kJ/g; the water absorbs extra heat from the hot metal of the can
33.0 kJ/g; incomplete combustion releases additional heat to the water
questions.explanation: q = 250 x 4.18 x 20.0 = 20 900 J = 20.9 kJ, and 20.9 / 0.80 = 26.1 kJ/g. Heat lost to the air and the can, and any incomplete combustion, make the measured value too low.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen. What are the products?
options: Carbon monoxide and water
Carbon and hydrogen gas
Methane and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: With plenty of oxygen, all the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen to water. Carbon monoxide and soot form only when oxygen is limited.

questions.stem: Octane, C₈H₁₈, is a major component of petrol. Which equation correctly shows its complete combustion?
options: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O
C₈H₁₈ + 8O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O
2C₈H₁₈ + 17O₂ → 16CO + 18H₂O
C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O
questions.explanation: Octane gives 8 CO₂ and 9 H₂O per molecule, needing 16 + 9 = 25 O atoms, or 12.5 O₂; doubling gives whole numbers. The equation with CO describes incomplete combustion.

questions.stem: A gas heater in a poorly ventilated room burns with a yellow, sooty flame. Why is this dangerous?
options: Soot absorbs all the oxygen in the room, so no carbon dioxide can form
Limited oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing toxic carbon monoxide
Excess oxygen causes the fuel to burn too hot, producing toxic carbon dioxide
The yellow flame shows that sulfur is burning, producing toxic hydrogen gas
questions.explanation: Without enough oxygen, some carbon forms carbon monoxide and soot (carbon) instead of carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and is poisonous; a clean blue flame shows complete combustion.

questions.stem: Which equation represents incomplete combustion of methane?
options: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂
2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH
questions.explanation: Producing carbon monoxide shows the carbon was only partly oxidised, so less oxygen was used: 3 O₂ for 2 CH₄ instead of 4. The equation giving CO₂ and H₂O is complete combustion.

questions.stem: Burning some types of coal produces sulfur dioxide. Why is this a problem?
options: Sulfur dioxide is a fuel, so burning coal wastes useful energy
Sulfur dioxide removes carbon dioxide from the air too quickly
Sulfur dioxide makes the combustion of coal endothermic overall
Sulfur dioxide forms acids in the atmosphere, causing acid rain
questions.explanation: Sulfur impurities burn to SO₂, which reacts with water and oxygen in the air to form sulfuric acid, falling as acid rain. Natural gas and biofuels contain little or no sulfur.

questions.stem: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) are produced in car engines whether petrol or bioethanol is used. Why?
options: At high engine temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen in air react
Both fuels contain nitrogen atoms, which are oxidised as the fuel burns
Both fuels burn incompletely, and nitrogen oxides replace carbon monoxide
Nitrogen oxides are formed from the water vapour produced by combustion
questions.explanation: The nitrogen comes from the air, not the fuel: at the high temperatures in an engine, N₂ and O₂ combine to form NO and NO₂. So switching fuel does not remove NOx emissions.

questions.stem: Compared with burning diesel from crude oil, what is a benefit of burning biodiesel?
options: It releases more energy per gram, because its molecules contain oxygen
It produces no nitrogen oxides, because it burns at a lower temperature
It produces less sulfur dioxide, because it contains almost no sulfur
It produces no carbon dioxide, because its carbon is not oxidised
questions.explanation: Biodiesel is made from plant oils with almost no sulfur, and it also tends to produce less soot and carbon monoxide. It still releases CO₂, and its oxygen content lowers, not raises, its energy per gram.

questions.stem: Why are biofuels sometimes described as close to carbon neutral?
options: The CO₂ released was recently absorbed from the air by photosynthesis
Biofuels contain no carbon, so burning them releases only water vapour
Burning biofuels absorbs CO₂ from the air, removing what fossil fuels release
The CO₂ from biofuels is heavier than air, so it stays near the ground
questions.explanation: Crops take in CO₂ as they grow, and burning the fuel returns about the same amount, so there is little net increase. Burning biofuels does release CO₂; it does not absorb it.

questions.stem: Why is bioethanol not completely carbon neutral in practice?
options: Ethanol is made from crude oil, so all of its carbon was buried long ago
Fossil fuels are often used to grow, harvest, transport and distil the crop
Ethanol releases more CO₂ per gram than the crop absorbed while it grew
Fermentation absorbs CO₂, so the overall cycle removes too much from the air
questions.explanation: Fertilisers, farm machinery, transport and heating for distillation usually rely on fossil fuels, adding CO₂ that was not absorbed by the crop. Fermentation itself releases CO₂.

questions.stem: Why are fossil fuels described as non-renewable?
options: They cannot be burned more than once, unlike biofuels, which can be reused
They are not made from living things, so they cannot be grown again
They release energy only once in their lifetime, while biofuels release it twice
They form over millions of years, far more slowly than we use them
questions.explanation: Coal, oil and gas formed from ancient organisms over geological time, so reserves are not replaced on a human timescale. Biofuels can be regrown each season. No fuel can be burned twice.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of producing biofuels from food crops?
options: It produces fuels that release no energy when they burn
It competes for farmland and water that could grow food
It increases the amount of sulfur released when fuel burns
It makes the fuel non-renewable, because crops take years to grow
questions.explanation: Large-scale crop-based biofuels use land, water and fertiliser that could produce food, and clearing land can release stored carbon. Biofuels contain little sulfur and are renewable.

questions.stem: Why is LPG (mainly propane and butane) suitable for portable barbecues and camping stoves?
options: It liquefies under moderate pressure, so much fuel fits in a small cylinder
It is a solid at room temperature, so it can be carried without a sealed container
It does not burn in air, so it is safe to store inside a tent or a car
It releases no carbon dioxide on combustion, so it can be burned anywhere
questions.explanation: Propane and butane liquefy under modest pressure, giving a compact, easily carried store of a fuel with a high energy content per gram. Like all hydrocarbons they are flammable and produce CO₂.

questions.stem: Hydrogen releases about 143 kJ per gram, far more than petrol, yet it is hard to use in cars. What is the main reason?
options: It produces large amounts of carbon monoxide, which is toxic in an enclosed engine
It releases its energy too slowly to power an engine, so cars accelerate poorly
It is a fossil fuel, so its supply is limited and it releases sulfur dioxide
As a gas it has very little energy per litre, so it must be compressed to store
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has a very high energy per gram but a very low density, so a large or high-pressure tank is needed to carry useful amounts. Its only combustion product is water.

questions.stem: Biodiesel can thicken and block fuel lines in cold weather more readily than diesel from crude oil. Which property of a fuel is this about?
options: How well it flows at low temperature
How much energy it releases per gram
How much sulfur it contains as impurity
How quickly it can be grown and replaced
questions.explanation: Suitability for purpose includes physical properties such as flow at low temperature and volatility, not just energy content. Biodiesel's esters tend to solidify at higher temperatures than diesel.

questions.stem: A remote mine site needs a fuel for generators that is easy to store for months, energy-dense by volume and safe to transport by road. Which fuel is most suitable?
options: Natural gas, which is stored as a gas at room temperature and pressure
Diesel, a liquid with high energy per litre and low volatility
Hydrogen gas, which has the highest energy per gram of any fuel
Biogas, which is made on site from waste with no storage needed
questions.explanation: Diesel is a liquid with a high energy per litre and low volatility, so it is relatively safe to transport and store. Gaseous fuels need large or pressurised containers, and hydrogen is hard to store despite its high energy per gram.

questions.stem: Which gas is the main component of both natural gas and biogas?
options: Carbon dioxide
Methane
Ethane
Propane
questions.explanation: Natural gas and biogas are both mostly methane, CH₄. Biogas also contains a large share of carbon dioxide, but CO₂ cannot burn, so it is not the fuel component.

questions.stem: What does the heat of combustion of a fuel measure?
options: The energy released when a set amount of the fuel burns completely
The temperature at which the fuel catches fire when heated in air
The minimum energy needed to start the fuel burning in oxygen
The speed at which the fuel burns in a plentiful supply of air
questions.explanation: Heat of combustion is the energy released per mole or per gram when a fuel burns completely in oxygen. The minimum energy needed to start the reaction is the activation energy, which is a different quantity.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that carbon dioxide is a product when a fuel burns?
options: The gas burns with a squeaky pop
The gas bleaches damp litmus paper
The gas turns limewater milky
The gas relights a glowing splint
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) to form a milky precipitate of calcium carbonate. Relighting a glowing splint is the test for oxygen, and a squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen.

questions.stem: Why is the combustion of a fuel exothermic?
options: More energy is absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds than is released forming the products' bonds
Energy is released both when the fuel's bonds break and when the new bonds in the products form
The fuel's bonds store energy, which is released as heat at the moment those bonds are broken
More energy is released forming the products' bonds than is absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and forming bonds always releases it. Combustion is exothermic because the bonds in CO₂ and H₂O release more energy as they form than is needed to break the bonds in the fuel and oxygen.

questions.stem: Methanol (CH₃OH, M = 32.0 g/mol) has a heat of combustion of 726 kJ/mol; propane (C₃H₈, M = 44.0 g/mol) has 2220 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: Propane releases about three times as much energy per gram as methanol
Both release about 23 kJ/g, because each is a carbon-based fuel
Propane releases about 50.5 kJ/g, a little over twice methanol's 22.7 kJ/g
Methanol releases about 50.5 kJ/g, a little over twice propane's 22.7 kJ/g
questions.explanation: Per gram: propane 2220 / 44.0 = 50.5 kJ/g and methanol 726 / 32.0 = 22.7 kJ/g, a ratio of about 2.2. The ratio of about three is per mole, not per gram, because propane molecules are heavier.

questions.stem: Ethanol has a heat of combustion of 1360 kJ/mol. Which thermochemical equation is correct?
options: 2C₂H₅OH(l) + 6O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)   ΔH = -1360 kJ/mol
C₂H₅OH(l) + 2O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)   ΔH = -1360 kJ/mol
C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)   ΔH = -1360 kJ/mol
C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)   ΔH = +1360 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: Combustion is exothermic, so ΔH is negative, and the value applies to 1 mol of ethanol as written. Doubling the equation doubles ΔH to -2720 kJ, and the equation with 2O₂ does not balance oxygen.

questions.stem: E10 petrol contains 10% ethanol. Why does a car usually travel slightly less far on a tank of E10 than on a tank of regular petrol?
options: Ethanol produces more CO₂ per litre, which reduces the engine's power
Ethanol releases less energy per litre than the petrol it replaces
Ethanol releases more energy per litre, so the engine runs too lean
Ethanol burns incompletely in all engines, so it forms soot instead
questions.explanation: Ethanol is partly oxidised already, so a litre of it releases less energy than a litre of petrol. Replacing 10% of the petrol with ethanol lowers the energy in a full tank slightly.

questions.stem: 1.00 kg of octane burns completely: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. Using M(C₈H₁₈) = 114.0 and M(CO₂) = 44.0 g/mol, what mass of CO₂ is produced?
questions.explanation: n(C₈H₁₈) = 1000 / 114.0 = 8.77 mol; each mole gives 8 mol CO₂, so n(CO₂) = 70.2 mol and mass = 70.2 x 44.0 = 3090 g. The CO₂ outweighs the fuel because oxygen from the air is added; 0.386 kg ignores the 1 : 8 ratio.

questions.stem: Why does burning natural gas in a power station release less CO₂ per kilojoule of energy than burning coal?
options: Coal burns more completely than natural gas, so more of its carbon is converted to CO₂
Natural gas is a biofuel, so the CO₂ it releases is absorbed again by growing plants
Methane has more hydrogen per carbon, and burning hydrogen releases energy without CO₂
Natural gas contains no carbon at all, so its only combustion product is water vapour
questions.explanation: Coal is mostly carbon, while each carbon in methane carries four hydrogen atoms whose combustion to water supplies much of the energy. Natural gas is still a fossil fuel and still produces CO₂.

questions.stem: Diesel engines and wood fires can release fine soot particles (particulates). What causes them, and why are they a health concern?
options: Incomplete combustion leaves unburnt carbon, which can lodge deep in the lungs
Complete combustion forms solid carbon dioxide, which settles in the airways
Sulfur in the fuel forms solid sulfur dust, which turns into acid in the eyes
Excess oxygen oxidises the engine metal, which forms dust that is breathed in
questions.explanation: When oxygen is limited, some carbon is not oxidised and escapes as tiny solid particles. Fine particulates can be breathed deep into the lungs and are linked to heart and lung disease.

questions.stem: Hydrogen produces only water when it burns. Why might a hydrogen-fuelled vehicle still be responsible for CO₂ emissions?
options: Burning hydrogen forms carbon monoxide, which is later oxidised to carbon dioxide
Hydrogen is stored in carbon tanks, which slowly burn along with the fuel
The hydrogen may have been made from fossil fuels such as natural gas or coal
Hydrogen combines with carbon in the air as it burns, forming carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Hydrogen must be manufactured. Making it from natural gas or coal releases CO₂, while electrolysis of water powered by renewable electricity does not. The combustion itself forms only water.

questions.stem: Why does the incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon release less energy than its complete combustion?
options: Incomplete combustion breaks more bonds in the fuel, which absorbs extra energy
Incomplete combustion is endothermic, so it takes in energy from the rest of the flame
Carbon monoxide puts out part of the flame, so less of the fuel reacts at all
Some carbon stops at CO, so the energy from oxidising CO to CO₂ is never released
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide and soot are only partly oxidised, so the energy that would be released by converting them to CO₂ is lost. Incomplete combustion is still exothermic, just less so.
